  • Core is a SQL expression toolkit — you build queries with Python expressions that map closely to SQL (select(users).where(...)), working with rows/tuples.
  • ORM sits on top of Core and adds class↔table mapping, identity map, change tracking, and relationships — you work with objects.

Use the ORM for application/business logic; drop to Core (or raw SQL) for bulk operations and complex analytical queries where object overhead hurts.

Key takeaway: Core = Pythonic SQL builder; ORM = object mapping on top. They interoperate, so you can mix them.

•

Q7. What is a connection pool and why does it matter?

Answerconnection poolKey takeaway

Answer:

Opening a new database connection (TCP + auth handshake) is expensive (milliseconds). A connection pool keeps a set of open connections and lends them to requests, returning them when done. SQLAlchemy's Engine pools by default.

Without pooling, a high-traffic API spends most of its time reconnecting and can exhaust the database's connection limit.

engine = create_engine(url, pool_size=10, max_overflow=20)

Key takeaway: Pools amortize the cost of connecting; tune pool_size/max_overflow to your concurrency and the DB's connection cap.

•

Q8. What is the Session in SQLAlchemy and how should its lifecycle be managed?

AnswerSessionidentity mapone per web requestKey takeaway

Answer:

The Session is the ORM's unit of work: it holds objects in an identity map, tracks their changes, and flushes them as SQL on commit(). Scope one Session to one logical operation — typically one per web request — and close it afterward.

with Session() as db:      # opened per request
    db.add(obj)
    db.commit()            # flushes + commits; session closed on exit

Sharing a single long-lived Session across threads/requests causes stale data and concurrency bugs.

Key takeaway: A Session is short-lived and per-request; open it, do the work, commit/rollback, close it.

•

Q9. How does an ORM protect against SQL injection?

Answerparameterized queriesKey takeaway

Answer:

ORMs (and the DBAPI) use parameterized queries (bind parameters): the SQL structure and the data are sent separately, so user input is never interpreted as SQL.

# Safe — value is bound, not interpolated
db.query(User).filter(User.email == user_input).all()

# DANGEROUS — never build SQL with string formatting
db.execute(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '{user_input}'")  # injectable

Key takeaway: Always pass values as parameters, never via f-strings/concatenation — parameterization is what neutralizes SQL injection. See [[best-practices-security]].

•

Q10. What is a database migration and why not just edit tables manually?

AnswermigrationAlembicKey takeaway

Answer:

A migration is a versioned, repeatable script describing a schema change (add column, create index, etc.). Tools like Alembic (for SQLAlchemy) generate and apply them in order.

Manual edits don't replicate across dev/staging/prod, aren't version-controlled, and can't be reliably rolled back. Migrations give you a reproducible, reviewable, reversible schema history that travels with your code.

alembic revision --autogenerate -m "add users.email index"
alembic upgrade head

Key takeaway: Migrations make schema changes versioned, reviewable, and reproducible across environments — never alter production schema by hand.

•

Q11. What is the difference between joinedload and selectinload?

AnswerjoinedloadoneselectinloadtwoKey takeaway

Answer:

Both prevent N+1, but differ in strategy:

  • joinedloademits one query with a JOIN. Great for one-to-one / small one-to-many; can multiply rows (and bytes) for large collections.
  • selectinloademits two queries (parent, then children via WHERE id IN (...)). Better for large one-to-many because it avoids row duplication.

Key takeaway: Use joinedload for small/single related objects, selectinload for large collections to avoid JOIN row-explosion.

•

Q12. When would you choose NoSQL over a relational database?

AnswerNoSQLrelationalKey takeaway

Answer:

Choose NoSQL when: - The schema is fluid or highly variable (document stores like MongoDB). - You need massive horizontal scale / high write throughput (Cassandra). - The access pattern is simple key-value at low latency (Redis). - Data is naturally graph-shaped (Neo4j).

Choose relational when you need joins, multi-row transactions, and strong consistency/integrity (orders, payments, inventory).

Key takeaway: Relational for structured, transactional, integrity-critical data; NoSQL for scale, flexibility, or specialized access patterns — many systems use both (polyglot persistence).

•

Q13. What is normalization vs denormalization?

AnswerNormalizationDenormalizationKey takeaway

Answer:

  • Normalization organizes tables to eliminate redundancy (each fact stored once), reducing update anomalies — the default for transactional (OLTP) systems.
  • Denormalization deliberately duplicates data to avoid joins and speed up reads — common in reporting/analytics (OLAP) and read-heavy systems.

Key takeaway: Normalize for write integrity, denormalize for read performance; it's a deliberate trade-off, not a default.

•

Q14. What is a deadlock and how do you avoid it?

AnswerdeadlockAvoid it byconsistent ordershortKey takeaway

Answer:

A deadlock happens when two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, so neither can proceed. The database detects it and kills one transaction (which you must retry).

Avoid it by: - Acquiring locks in a consistent order across the codebase. - Keeping transactions short. - Using lower isolation levels where safe. - Adding retry logic for the victim transaction.

Key takeaway: Deadlocks come from inconsistent lock ordering and long transactions — order access consistently, keep transactions short, and retry the loser.

•

Q15. What is eager vs lazy loading?

AnswerLazy loadingEager loadingKey takeaway

Answer:

  • Lazy loading (default) — related objects are fetched only when first accessed. Convenient, but accessing them in a loop causes the N+1 problem.
  • Eager loadingrelated objects are fetched up front in the same operation (joinedload/selectinload), avoiding extra round-trips.

Key takeaway: Lazy is convenient for single objects; switch to eager loading the moment you iterate over a collection's relationships. See Q2.

•

Q16. What is the difference between flush and commit?

Answerflush()commit()commitsautoflushesKey takeaway

Answer:

  • flush() sends pending SQL (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) to the database within the current transaction, so the DB can assign primary keys and enforce constraints — but nothing is made permanent and it can still be rolled back.
  • commit() flushes and commits the transaction, making changes durable and visible to other connections. It also flushes automatically first.

By default a Session autoflushes before each query, so your pending changes are visible to your own subsequent queries without an explicit flush.

db.add(user)
db.flush()          # INSERT runs now → user.id is populated, still rollback-able
order.user_id = user.id
db.commit()         # both rows committed atomically

Key takeaway: flush = "emit SQL now, still inside the transaction" (e.g. to get a generated id); commit = "make it permanent." Commit flushes for you.

•

Q17. What is the identity map and the unit-of-work pattern?

AnswerIdentity mapexactly oneUnit of worktracks all changesKey takeaway

Answer:

  • Identity mapwithin one Session, each database row is represented by exactly one Python object, keyed by primary key. Querying the same row twice returns the same object, so changes are consistent and there's no duplicate state.
  • Unit of workthe Session tracks all changes to those objects and emits the minimal set of SQL in the correct order at flush/commit, instead of you writing each statement.
a = db.get(User, 1)
b = db.get(User, 1)
assert a is b        # identity map: same object, served from the session's cache

Key takeaway: The Session is an identity map + unit of work — one object per row, automatic change tracking, batched SQL on commit. See [[database-session-lifecycle]].

•

Q18. Optimistic vs pessimistic locking — how do you prevent lost updates?

Answerlost updateOptimisticPessimisticKey takeaway

Answer:

A lost update: two transactions read the same row, both modify it, and the second overwrites the first. Two defenses:

  • Optimistic (low contention): add a version column; on write, check the version hasn't changed and bump it. A mismatch → 0 rows updated → raise a 409 and retry. SQLAlchemy automates this via __mapper_args__ = {"version_id_col": version}.
  • Pessimistic (high contention, money): lock the row up front with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (with_for_update()) so others block until you commit.
row = db.execute(select(Account).where(Account.id == aid).with_for_update()).scalar_one()

Key takeaway: Optimistic locking (version column, 409 on conflict) scales for rare conflicts; pessimistic (FOR UPDATE) suits hot, high-stakes rows. See the worked scenarios in [[fastapi-threading-orm-scenarios]].

•

Q19. What do relationship cascades control?

AnswerrelatedKey takeaway

Answer:

Cascades define what happens to related objects when you act on a parent — most importantly on delete. Configure via relationship(..., cascade=..., passive_deletes=...):

  • save-update, merge (default) — children added to the session follow the parent.
  • all, delete-orphan — deleting the parent deletes its children; removing a child from the collection deletes it.
  • passive_deletes=True — defer deletion to the DB's ON DELETE CASCADE foreign key instead of loading and deleting children in Python (much faster for large sets).
class User(Base):
    posts = relationship("Post", cascade="all, delete-orphan", passive_deletes=True)

Key takeaway: Cascades decide whether deletes/saves propagate to children; use delete-orphan for owned children and passive_deletes + a DB-level ON DELETE CASCADE for performance.

•

Q20. How do you efficiently insert/update thousands of rows?

Answer:

Adding objects one-by-one with a commit() per row is the classic slow path (a round-trip + the unit-of-work overhead each time). Faster options, in order:

# Better: many adds, ONE commit
db.add_all([User(**d) for d in rows]); db.commit()

# Faster: bulk operations (skip most ORM unit-of-work machinery)
db.bulk_insert_mappings(User, rows)         # 1.x style
db.execute(insert(User), rows)              # 2.0 style — executemany under the hood
db.commit()

# Fastest for huge loads: the DB's native bulk loader (e.g. PostgreSQL COPY)

Trade-off: bulk methods bypass identity map, relationship cascades, and events — use them for plain data loads, not when you need ORM features.

Key takeaway: Batch the commit, then reach for bulk inserts / executemany, then native COPY — each step trades ORM convenience for throughput.

•

Q21. How do you diagnose a slow query?

AnswerFindExplainSeq ScanIndex ScanFix

Answer:

  1. Find it — log slow queries (SQLAlchemy before/after_cursor_execute events, or the DB's slow-query log).
  2. Explain it — run EXPLAIN ANALYZE <query> to see the plan: is it a Seq Scan (full table) where you expected an Index Scan? Are row estimates wildly off?
  3. Fix it — add/adjust an index, rewrite the query, eager-load to kill N+1, select only needed columns, or add LIMIT.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42 AND status = 'paid';
-- "Seq Scan on orders ..." → missing index on (user_id, status)

Key takeaway: Measure, don't guess — EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows whether the planner uses your indexes; a sequential scan on a large filtered table is the usual smoking gun.

•

Q22. How does a composite index work, and what's the leftmost-prefix rule?

Answercomposite indexleftmost-prefix rulecovering indexKey takeaway

Answer:

A composite index covers multiple columns in order, e.g. (user_id, status, created_at). The leftmost-prefix rule: the index can serve queries that filter on a prefix of those columns, left to right.

Query filterUses the index?
user_id✅ (prefix)
user_id, status✅ (prefix)
user_id, status, created_at✅ (full)
status alone❌ (skips the leftmost column)
created_at alone❌

A covering index additionally includes all columns the query needs, so the DB answers it from the index alone ("index-only scan") without touching the table.

Key takeaway: Order composite-index columns by how you filter (most selective / always-present first); only queries using a left-anchored prefix benefit.

•

Q23. How do you scale a database for reads and for writes?

AnswerRead scaling → replicasreplicasreplication lagBefore eitherKey takeaway

Answer:

  • Read scaling → replicas. A primary handles writes and streams changes to read replicas; route read-only queries there. Watch for replication lag (a replica may serve slightly stale data — read-after-write may need to hit the primary).
  • Write scaling → sharding / partitioning. Split data across shards by a key (user_id, region) so each holds a subset. Powerful but adds complexity: cross-shard joins and transactions are hard.
  • Before either: caching (Redis), connection pooling, indexes, and query tuning often remove the need to scale out at all.

Key takeaway: Scale reads with replicas (mind the lag), scale writes with sharding/partitioning (mind cross-shard complexity) — but exhaust caching and query tuning first.

•

Q24. What is a detached instance / DetachedInstanceError?

Answerclosesexpired/detachedFixesEager-loadinside

Answer:

After a Session closes (or commit() with the default expire_on_commit=True), its objects are expired/detached. Accessing a not-yet-loaded attribute or a lazy relationship then raises DetachedInstanceError — there's no live session to issue the SQL. Common when you return ORM objects from a function after its with Session() block ends.

Fixes: - Set expire_on_commit=False so already-loaded attributes stay usable after commit. - Eager-load everything you'll need before the session closes. - Convert to a plain dict / Pydantic model inside the session scope (e.g. FastAPI response_model with from_attributes=True).

Key takeaway: Don't touch lazy attributes on an object whose Session has closed — materialize what you need (eager-load or serialize) before the session ends, or keep attributes alive with expire_on_commit=False.

•

Q25. What changes when you use async SQLAlchemy?

Answereager-loadKey takeaway

Answer:

With AsyncSession / create_async_engine (and an async driver like asyncpg), every database operation must be awaited, and you cannot rely on implicit lazy loading — touching an un-loaded relationship outside an awaited call raises MissingGreenlet. So you must eager-load (selectinload/joinedload) anything you'll access, including for serialization.

async with AsyncSession(engine) as db:
    result = await db.execute(
        select(User).where(User.id == uid).options(selectinload(User.posts))
    )
    user = result.scalar_one()      # user.posts already loaded — safe to serialize

Key takeaway: Async ORM removes the "lazy load just works" safety net — await everything and eager-load relationships explicitly. See the worked async pitfalls in [[fastapi-threading-orm-scenarios]].

API Consumption & Webhooks

Source: 01_Python/33_API_Consumption_and_Webhooks/

•

Q1. What is the difference between consuming an API and building one?

AnswerBuildingConsumingKey takeaway

Answer:

  • Building an API (server side) means exposing endpoints that accept requests and return responses — the job of frameworks like FastAPI or Flask.
  • Consuming an API (client side) means acting as the client that calls someone else's endpoints over HTTP and processes the response.

A single service is usually both: a FastAPI backend (server) that calls a payment provider's REST API (client) to charge a card.

Key takeaway: "Consuming" puts you on the client side of HTTP — you make the request and handle the response, retries, auth, and failures.

•

Q2. Why use requests.Session() instead of calling requests.get() directly?

AnswerReuses connectionsPersists stateKey takeaway

Answer:

A bare requests.get() opens a brand-new TCP (and TLS) connection every call and throws it away. A Session:

  1. Reuses connections via an underlying urllib3 connection pool — big latency win when hitting the same host repeatedly.
  2. Persists stateheaders, cookies, and auth across requests.
  3. Lets you set defaults once (base headers, timeouts via adapters).
with requests.Session() as s:
    s.headers.update({"Authorization": "Bearer TOKEN"})
    s.get("https://api.example.com/v1/user")     # connection opened
    s.get("https://api.example.com/v1/profile")  # connection reused

Key takeaway: Use a Session whenever you make more than one request to the same host — it pools connections and persists auth.

•

Q3. When should you use httpx instead of requests?

AnswerasyncKey takeaway

Answer:

Use httpx when you need async I/O (e.g. inside FastAPI, an asyncio app, or to fire many requests concurrently). requests is synchronous and blocking — calling it inside an async def blocks the event loop and destroys concurrency.

httpx offers: - A near-identical sync API to requests (easy migration). - A true async client (httpx.AsyncClient). - HTTP/2 support, built-in timeouts, and connection pooling.

async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10.0) as client:
    responses = await asyncio.gather(
        client.get("https://api.example.com/a"),
        client.get("https://api.example.com/b"),
    )

Key takeaway: requests for simple sync scripts; httpx when you're in an async context or need concurrency/HTTP-2.

•

Q4. Why must you always set a timeout on outgoing requests?

AnswerforeverKey takeaway

Answer:

By default requests waits forever for a response. If the remote server hangs (slow, overloaded, or malicious), your thread/worker is blocked indefinitely. Under load this exhausts your worker pool and cascades into a full outage — your service goes down because a dependency went down.

requests.get(url, timeout=5)          # total timeout
requests.get(url, timeout=(3, 10))    # (connect timeout, read timeout)

Key takeaway: A missing timeout is one of the most common production outages. Always set one; consider separate connect/read timeouts.

•

Q5. What is the difference between response.raise_for_status() and checking status_code?

AnswerKey takeaway

Answer:

  • response.status_code lets you branch manually (if response.status_code == 404: ...).
  • response.raise_for_status() raises an HTTPError automatically for any 4xx/5xx response, so you can rely on try/except instead of remembering to check.

Note: requests only raises for HTTP error statuses when you ask it to. A connection failure or timeout raises a different exception (ConnectionError, Timeout) regardless.

try:
    r = requests.get(url, timeout=5)
    r.raise_for_status()
    data = r.json()
except requests.HTTPError as e:        # 4xx / 5xx
    ...
except requests.RequestException as e: # network/timeout/DNS
    ...

Key takeaway: raise_for_status() converts bad HTTP statuses into exceptions; network-level failures raise separately, so catch RequestException as the base.

•

Q6. What are common HTTP status codes a client should handle?

AnswernotKey takeaway

Answer:

CodeMeaningClient action
200 / 201OK / CreatedSuccess
204No ContentSuccess, no body to parse
301 / 302RedirectUsually followed automatically
400Bad RequestFix the payload; do not retry blindly
401UnauthorizedRefresh/supply credentials
403ForbiddenPermission issue — not retryable
404Not FoundResource missing
422Unprocessable EntityValidation error (common with FastAPI)
429Too Many RequestsBack off, honor Retry-After
5xxServer errorRetry with backoff (often transient)

Key takeaway: Retry only transient failures (429, 5xx, network errors). Retrying a 400/401/403 just wastes calls — fix the request instead.

•

Q7. How do you implement retries with exponential backoff, and why "exponential"?

AnswerExponentialjitterKey takeaway

Answer:

Retry transient failures with increasing delays so you don't hammer a struggling server. Exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s…) spreads load far better than fixed delays. Add jitter (randomness) so many clients don't retry in lockstep and create a thundering herd.

from tenacity import retry, stop_after_attempt, wait_exponential

@retry(stop=stop_after_attempt(5),
       wait=wait_exponential(multiplier=1, min=2, max=30))
def fetch():
    r = requests.get(url, timeout=5)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()

Key takeaway: Exponential backoff + jitter avoids overwhelming a recovering service and prevents synchronized retry storms.

•

Q8. What is the difference between polling and webhooks?

AnswerPollingWebhookspushesKey takeaway

Answer:

  • Pollingthe client repeatedly asks the server "is it done yet?" on a schedule. Simple but wasteful — most calls return "no change," and you trade latency (poll interval) for load.
  • Webhooksthe client registers a callback URL once; the server pushes an HTTP POST to that URL when an event happens. Near-real-time and far fewer wasted calls.

Polling is "pull"; webhooks are "push." Webhooks invert the relationship — your app becomes a server receiving the provider's request.

Key takeaway: Webhooks replace inefficient "are we there yet?" polling with event-driven push, at the cost of needing a publicly reachable, secured endpoint.

•

Q9. How do you secure a webhook endpoint?

AnswerVerify the signatureraw bytesUse the raw bodyCheck timestampsReturn 2xx fast

Answer:

Your webhook URL is public, so anyone could POST fake events. Defenses:

  1. Verify the signature. Providers sign the raw request body with a shared secret (usually HMAC-SHA256) and send it in a header (e.g. Stripe-Signature). Recompute the HMAC over the raw bytes and compare with a constant-time check.
  2. Use the raw body, not the parsed JSON — re-serializing changes bytes and breaks the signature.
  3. Check timestamps to reject replayed old events.
  4. Return 2xx fast, then process asynchronously (offload to a task queue) so the provider doesn't time out and retry.
import hmac, hashlib

def verify(payload: bytes, signature: str, secret: str) -> bool:
    expected = hmac.new(secret.encode(), payload, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    return hmac.compare_digest(expected, signature)

Key takeaway: Always verify the HMAC signature over the raw body with hmac.compare_digest, and acknowledge quickly while processing in the background.

•

Q10. Why must webhook handlers be idempotent?

Answerat-least-onceretryevent IDKey takeaway

Answer:

Providers guarantee at-least-once delivery: if your endpoint is slow or returns a non-2xx, they retry, so the same event can arrive multiple times. If your handler isn't idempotent, you double-charge, double-email, or double-insert.

Make it idempotent by deduplicating on the provider's event ID:

if already_processed(event["id"]):   # e.g. row in a "seen_events" table
    return {"status": "ok"}          # ack, do nothing
process(event)
mark_processed(event["id"])

Key takeaway: Webhooks (and most distributed messaging) are at-least-once — dedupe on a unique event ID so re-delivery is harmless. See [[task-queues-idempotency]].

•

Q11. How do you handle pagination when consuming a large API?

AnswerOffset/limitPage numberCursor / keysetKey takeaway

Answer:

APIs page large result sets. Three common styles:

  • Offset/limit?limit=100&offset=200 — simple but slow and inconsistent on changing data.
  • Page number?page=3 — convenient, same drawbacks as offset.
  • Cursor / keysetresponse returns a next_cursor token you pass back — stable and efficient for large/streaming data.

Iterate until there's no next page; a generator keeps memory flat:

def fetch_all(url, params):
    while url:
        r = requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=10)
        r.raise_for_status()
        data = r.json()
        yield from data["items"]
        url = data.get("next")     # follow the cursor/next-link
        params = None

Key takeaway: Detect the pagination style, loop until exhausted, and prefer cursor-based pagination for large datasets; stream with a generator to avoid loading everything in memory.

•

Q12. What is rate limiting and how do you respect it as a client?

Answer429 Too Many RequestsRetry-AfterKey takeaway

Answer:

APIs cap how many requests you may send per window (e.g. 100/min). Exceed it and you get 429 Too Many Requests. To be a good client:

  1. Read rate-limit headers (X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset).
  2. On a 429, honor the Retry-After header instead of guessing.
  3. Throttle proactively (token-bucket / leaky-bucket) so you stay under the limit.
if r.status_code == 429:
    wait = int(r.headers.get("Retry-After", 1))
    time.sleep(wait)

Key takeaway: Treat 429 as "slow down," obey Retry-After, and throttle client-side so you rarely hit the limit at all.

•

Q13. What are the common API authentication schemes you'll encounter as a client?

AnswerKey takeaway

Answer:

SchemeHow you send itNotes
API keyHeader or query paramSimplest; keep it secret
Bearer token (OAuth2/JWT)Authorization: Bearer <token>Tokens expire → refresh them
Basic authAuthorization: Basic base64(user:pass)Only over HTTPS
HMAC signingSign request with secretUsed by AWS, some webhooks
mTLSClient TLS certificateHigh-security, service-to-service

For OAuth2 you typically exchange credentials for a short-lived access token, send it as a Bearer header, and refresh when it expires (401).

Key takeaway: Most public APIs use API keys or OAuth2 Bearer tokens; store secrets in env/config (never in code), and handle token refresh on 401.

•

Q14. How should you store and manage API keys and secrets?

AnswerNeverKey takeaway

Answer:

  • Never commit secrets to source control or hard-code them.
  • Load from environment variables, a .env file (via python-dotenv or pydantic-settings), or a secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault).
  • Rotate keys periodically and scope them to least privilege.
  • Add .env to .gitignore.
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    api_key: str
    class Config:
        env_file = ".env"

settings = Settings()

Key takeaway: Secrets come from the environment/secret store, never the codebase — pydantic-settings gives you typed, validated config loading. See [[best-practices-security]].

•

Q15. What is a circuit breaker and when would you use one?

Answercircuit breakerClosedOpenHalf-openKey takeaway

Answer:

A circuit breaker stops sending requests to a dependency that is clearly failing, instead of retrying into a black hole. Like an electrical breaker it has three states:

  • Closedcalls flow normally; failures are counted.
  • Openafter too many failures it "trips" — calls fail fast immediately (no network call) for a cooldown period.
  • Half-openafter cooldown it lets a few trial calls through; success closes the circuit, failure re-opens it.

This prevents a failing downstream service from tying up all your workers and gives it room to recover.

Key takeaway: Retries handle transient blips; circuit breakers handle a dependency that's down — fail fast and protect your own service from cascading failure.

•

Q16. What's the difference between connect timeout and read timeout?

AnswerConnect timeoutRead timeoutKey takeaway

Answer:

  • Connect timeoutmax time to establish the TCP/TLS connection to the server. A short value (2–3s) catches unreachable hosts quickly.
  • Read timeoutmax time to wait between bytes of the response once connected. Set higher for slow but valid endpoints.
requests.get(url, timeout=(3, 30))  # 3s to connect, 30s to read

A total/overall timeout (single number) covers both phases combined.

Key takeaway: Separate connect and read timeouts let you fail fast on dead hosts while still allowing legitimately slow responses to complete.

Auth & Security

Source: 01_Python/34_Auth_and_Security/

Q&A drill for the consolidated [[auth-and-security]] reference. Cross-links: [[fastapi]], [[best-practices]], [[pydantic]], [[api-consumption]].

•

Q1. What's the difference between authentication and authorization?

AnswerAuthentication (AuthN)401 UnauthorizedAuthorization (AuthZ)403 ForbiddenKey takeaway

Answer:

  • Authentication (AuthN) = "who are you?" — verifying identity (password, token, MFA). Failure → 401 Unauthorized.
  • Authorization (AuthZ) = "what are you allowed to do?" — checking permissions for a resource/action (RBAC, scopes, ownership). Failure → 403 Forbidden.

They run in order: authenticate first, then authorize. 401 means "I don't know you, log in"; 403 means "I know you, but you can't do this."

Key takeaway: AuthN establishes identity; AuthZ gates what that identity may do — different steps, different status codes.

•

Q2. Why can't you store passwords with SHA-256, and what should you use?

Answerslow, salted, adaptiveArgon2idbcryptscryptKey takeaway

Answer:

SHA-256 is a fast, general-purpose hash — a GPU computes billions per second, so a leaked table is brute-forced quickly, and it has no built-in salt. Passwords need a slow, salted, adaptive hash: Argon2id (modern first choice), bcrypt (proven default), or scrypt — tuned so one hash takes ~250–500 ms.

from passlib.context import CryptContext
pwd = CryptContext(schemes=["argon2", "bcrypt"], deprecated="auto")
h = pwd.hash("s3cret")          # salt auto-generated & embedded
pwd.verify("s3cret", h)         # constant-time

Key takeaway: Use a deliberately slow, salted password hash (argon2/bcrypt) — never md5/sha1/sha256.

•

Q3. What are a salt and a pepper?

AnswerSaltPepperoutsideKey takeaway

Answer:

  • Salta unique random value per password, mixed in before hashing. Defeats rainbow tables and ensures two identical passwords hash differently. bcrypt/argon2 generate and store it inside the hash automatically.
  • Pepperan app-wide secret kept outside the database (env/HSM), HMAC'd in before hashing. If only the DB leaks, the hashes are still useless without the pepper. Defense in depth.

Key takeaway: Salt (per-password, in the hash) stops precomputation; pepper (app-wide, out of the DB) hardens against DB-only leaks.

•

Q4. Walk through how a JWT works and its three parts.

AnswersignedHeaderPayloadnot encryptedSignature

Answer:

A JWT is a compact, URL-safe, signed token: HEADER.PAYLOAD.SIGNATURE (three base64url segments).

  • Header{"alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT"}
  • Payloadclaims like sub, exp, iat, iss, aud, role (readable — only base64, not encrypted).
  • SignatureHMAC-SHA256(header.payload, SECRET); only the key-holder can forge it.

Flow: client logs in → server signs a JWT → client sends Authorization: Bearer <token> → server verifies the signature and exp on every request, statelessly.

Key takeaway: A JWT is signed-not-encrypted; the server trusts it because the signature can't be forged — never put secrets in the payload.

•

Q5. What is the JWT alg=none (and alg confusion) attack, and how do you prevent it?

Answeralg=nonealg confusion (RS256→HS256)never trusting the token's own algKey takeaway

Answer:

  • alg=nonethe attacker sets the header's alg to none and strips the signature; a naive verifier that "trusts the header" accepts an unsigned token.
  • alg confusion (RS256→HS256)the attacker switches an asymmetric token to HS256 and signs it using the public key as the HMAC secret.

Prevent both by never trusting the token's own alg — always pass an explicit allow-list to the decoder:

jwt.decode(token, key, algorithms=["HS256"])   # pin it; never decode without algorithms=

Key takeaway: Always decode with an explicit algorithms=[...] allow-list; the header's alg is attacker-controlled.

•

Q6. HS256 vs RS256 — when do you use each?

AnswerHS256 (symmetric)single serviceRS256 (asymmetric)privatepublic

Answer:

  • HS256 (symmetric)one shared secret both signs and verifies. Simple; ideal for a single service that issues and checks its own tokens.
  • RS256 (asymmetric)a private key signs, the public key verifies. Use across microservices or with a third-party identity provider, so verifiers never hold the signing key. ES256 is the same idea with smaller elliptic-curve keys.

Key takeaway: HS256 for a single trusted service; RS256/ES256 when multiple/untrusted parties must verify but not mint tokens.

•

Q7. Sessions vs JWTs — trade-offs?

AnswerInstantHardKey takeaway

Answer:

Server-side sessionsStateless JWT
StateStored server-side (Redis/DB); client holds an opaque idNone; all data in the signed token
RevocationInstant (delete the session)Hard (valid until exp; needs a denylist)
ScalingNeeds a shared storeTrivial — any node verifies
Best forBrowser apps, easy logoutAPIs, mobile, microservices

Key takeaway: Sessions give easy revocation at the cost of server state; JWTs give stateless scale at the cost of revocation — many apps combine both (short JWT + refresh token).

•

Q8. Since a JWT can't be revoked before it expires, how do you handle logout/revocation?

AnswerShort access tokensRefresh-token rotationjti denylistKey takeaway

Answer:

Three common approaches: 1. Short access tokens (15–60 min) so a leaked token dies quickly on its own. 2. Refresh-token rotation — keep the access token short and revoke by deleting the long-lived refresh token server-side. 3. jti denylist — give each token a unique id and check a (Redis) blocklist on each request (reintroduces some state).

Key takeaway: You can't un-issue a signed JWT, so design for short lifetimes + a revocable refresh token (or a jti denylist) rather than relying on the access token alone.

•

Q9. How does refresh-token rotation work, and why detect reuse?

Answernewpreviously-rotatedrevoke the entire token familyhashedKey takeaway

Answer:

On /refresh, you issue a new access token and a new refresh token, invalidating the old refresh token (one-time use). If a previously-rotated refresh token is presented again, that means two parties hold it — likely theft — so you revoke the entire token family and force re-login. Store refresh tokens hashed (like passwords) so a DB leak can't replay them.

Key takeaway: Rotate refresh tokens on every use, hash them at rest, and treat reuse of a rotated token as a theft signal.

•

Q10. OAuth2 vs OpenID Connect?

AnswerOAuth2authorizationOpenID Connect (OIDC)authenticationID token

Answer:

  • OAuth2 is an authorization framework — it grants an app limited, delegated access to a resource on a user's behalf (without sharing the password).
  • OpenID Connect (OIDC) sits on top of OAuth2 and adds authentication via an ID token (a JWT identifying the user).

Rule of thumb: OAuth2 = access (a key card), OIDC = identity (a passport). "Sign in with Google" is OIDC.

Key takeaway: OAuth2 authorizes access; OIDC adds who-the-user-is on top.

•

Q11. Which OAuth2 grant type do you use for an SPA/mobile app vs a backend service?

AnswerAuthorization Code + PKCEClient CredentialsRefresh TokenImplicitPassword/ROPC

Answer:

  • Authorization Code + PKCEfor user login from a public client (SPA/mobile/web). PKCE prevents auth-code interception and is mandatory for public clients.
  • Client Credentialsfor machine-to-machine (no user); the service authenticates with its own id/secret.
  • Refresh Tokento renew access tokens.
  • Avoid Implicit (deprecated) and Password/ROPC (legacy; first-party only).

Key takeaway: Authorization Code + PKCE for users, Client Credentials for service-to-service.

•

Q12. RBAC vs ABAC, and what's the most commonly forgotten authorization check?

AnswerRBACABACKey takeaway

Answer:

  • RBACpermissions attach to roles; users get roles (admin/editor/viewer). Coarse and simple.
  • ABACdecisions from attributes of user + resource + context ("editors may edit docs in their own department").

The most-forgotten check is object-level (ownership) authorization — confirming the user owns this specific record, not just that their role can read "some" records. It's OWASP's #1 ("Broken Object Level Authorization").

if order.user_id != current_user.id and not current_user.is_admin:
    raise HTTPException(403, "Not your order")

Key takeaway: Beyond role checks, always verify the user is authorized for the specific object being accessed.

•

Q13. Why use secrets instead of random, and why hmac.compare_digest instead of ==?

Answershort-circuitsconstant timeKey takeaway

Answer:

  • random is a deterministic Mersenne Twister — predictable from a few outputs, so it's unsafe for tokens/keys. secrets is a CSPRNG: secrets.token_urlsafe(32).
  • == on strings short-circuits on the first differing byte, so its timing leaks how much of a secret matched — a timing attack can recover it byte by byte. hmac.compare_digest compares in constant time.

Key takeaway: secrets for generating security values, hmac.compare_digest for comparing them.

•

Q14. How do you prevent SQL injection and command injection in Python?

AnswerSQLCommandKey takeaway

Answer:

  • SQLnever build queries with f-strings; pass parameters and let the driver bind/escape them:
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = %s", (email,))   # ✅
  • Commandnever shell=True with user input (or os.system/eval/exec); pass a list of args:
subprocess.run(["ping", "-c", "1", host], check=True)           # ✅

Both follow one rule: keep attacker DATA from being interpreted as CODE.

Key takeaway: Parameterize SQL and use list-form subprocess (no shell); never interpolate user input into an interpreter.

•

Q15. What's the danger with pickle / yaml.load, and the safe alternative?

Answerexecute arbitrary codeKey takeaway

Answer:

pickle.loads() on untrusted data and yaml.load() (full loader) can execute arbitrary code during deserialization. Use data-only formats: json.loads(), or yaml.safe_load(). Never unpickle anything you didn't produce yourself.

Key takeaway: Insecure deserialization = remote code execution; prefer JSON / yaml.safe_load, never pickle untrusted input.

•

Q16. What is CSRF, and how is it different from XSS? How do you defend against each?

AnswerXSSContent-Security-PolicyCSRFSameSiteCSRF token

Answer:

  • XSSinjected JavaScript runs in your page and can steal tokens or act as the user. Defend with output encoding/escaping, a Content-Security-Policy, and HttpOnly cookies; never render untrusted HTML.
  • CSRFa malicious site tricks the victim's browser into sending an authenticated request using its cookie. Defend with SameSite cookies plus a CSRF token on state-changing requests. Bearer-token (header) APIs are largely immune because a cross-origin site can't set the Authorization header.

Key takeaway: XSS runs hostile code in your page (escape output, CSP); CSRF rides the user's cookie (SameSite + CSRF tokens). Header-based token auth sidesteps CSRF.

•

Q17. Is CORS a security mechanism? What does a safe config look like?

AnswernotKey takeaway

Answer:

CORS is not a server-side protection — it only relaxes the browser's same-origin policy to say which origins may read responses. It does nothing for non-browser clients and isn't auth. A safe config lists explicit origins and never combines "*" with credentials:

app.add_middleware(CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["https://myapp.com"],   # not ["*"] with allow_credentials=True
    allow_credentials=True)

Key takeaway: CORS controls which browser origins can read responses — it's not authentication, and wildcard-with-credentials is unsafe/invalid.

•

Q18. Where should secrets live, and what do you do if one is committed to git?

Answerrotate it immediatelyKey takeaway

Answer:

Secrets belong in environment variables / a secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault), never in code. Keep a .env.example with blank values; .gitignore the real .env. Validate required secrets at startup (Pydantic BaseSettings + SecretStr so they don't print in logs).

If a secret was committed: rotate it immediately (assume it's already scraped), then purge it from history (git filter-repo/BFG) and force-push. Deleting the file alone is not enough — it's still in history.

Key takeaway: Secrets from env/vault, never committed; if leaked, rotate first, then scrub history.

•

Q19. How do you authenticate one backend service to another?

AnswerHMAC-signed requestsOAuth2 client credentialsmTLSKey takeaway

Answer:

Options, roughly increasing in strength: - API keys (stored hashed, compared in constant time) — simplest; rotate regularly. - HMAC-signed requests — proves integrity + authenticity; add a timestamp/nonce to stop replay (used by webhooks). - OAuth2 client credentials — standard short-lived tokens for microservices. - mTLS — both sides present certificates; strong zero-trust option.

Key takeaway: For service-to-service, prefer HMAC signing or OAuth2 client credentials (or mTLS) over a static shared key — and always compare secrets in constant time.

•

Q20. Name the JWT validation checks you must perform on every request.

AnswerSignatureexpiss / audRequired claims presentjti not in the denylist

Answer:

  1. Signaturewith an explicit algorithms=[...] allow-list (defeats alg=none/confusion).
  2. expreject expired tokens (and nbf/iat if present).
  3. iss / audconfirm the token was issued by you and intended for your service.
  4. Required claims present (e.g. sub) and the user still exists/active.
  5. (If revocable) jti not in the denylist.

Key takeaway: Verify signature with a pinned algorithm plus exp, iss, aud, and required claims — a valid signature alone is not enough.

•

Q21. What are the headline security misconfigurations to avoid in a Python web app?

AnswerKey takeaway

Answer:

  • debug=True / verbose stack traces exposed to clients in production.
  • Permissive CORS ("*" + credentials) or wide-open security groups.
  • Default/weak credentials and missing rate limiting on auth endpoints.
  • Returning ORM models directly (leaking internal fields) instead of a response schema.
  • Missing security headers (HSTS, CSP, X-Frame-Options) and serving over plain HTTP.

Key takeaway: Ship with debug=False, generic errors, locked-down CORS, rate limiting, response schemas, and security headers — misconfiguration is OWASP A05.

•

Q22. What security tooling would you put in CI?

Answerbanditpip-auditsafetyDependabot/Renovatedetect-secrets

Answer:

  • bandit (or ruff --select S) — SAST that flags eval, shell=True, weak hashes, hardcoded passwords.
  • pip-audit / safetyscan dependencies for known CVEs; Dependabot/Renovate for auto-upgrade PRs.
  • detect-secrets / gitleakssecret scanning, ideally also as a pre-commit hook.

Key takeaway: Layer SAST (bandit), dependency scanning (pip-audit), and secret scanning (detect-secrets) across pre-commit and CI.

Revision tip: the whole topic reduces to three questions at every trust boundary — who are you? (hash passwords, validate tokens), what may you do? (per-object authz), and is this input safe? (parameterize, allow-list, never deserialize untrusted data) — with secrets kept out of code and crypto left to vetted libraries.

DSA Interview25 sections

Data Structures & Algorithms — Interview Questions

Consolidated interview Q&A — one grouped bank instead of a file per topic. Each topic's reference guide still lives in its 01_Python/<NN_Topic>/ folder.

Data Structures & Algorithms

Source: 01_Python/27_DSA/

•

Q1. How do you approach a coding interview problem?

AnswerClarifyExamplesBrute forceOptimizeCode

Answer:

A repeatable framework:

  1. Clarifyask about input constraints, ranges, types, duplicates, and the expected output format.
  2. Exampleswork through 2–3 examples by hand, including edge cases (empty, single element, all equal).
  3. Brute forcestate the obvious O(n²)/O(2ⁿ) solution first to show you understand the problem.
  4. Optimizelook for a pattern: sorted? → two pointers / binary search; subarray? → sliding window; "min/max ways"? → DP; overlapping work? → memoize.
  5. Codewrite clean, modular code with helper functions.
  6. Testtrace through examples and edge cases.
  7. Complexitystate final time and space complexity.

Key takeaway: Communicate at every step. Interviewers grade your reasoning and communication as much as the final code.

•

Q2. What is Big O notation and why do we drop constants?

Answerdominant termO(a + b)Key takeaway

Answer:

Big O describes how an algorithm's running time (or space) grows as input size n grows, focusing on the dominant term for large n. We drop constants and lower-order terms because they're irrelevant asymptotically: O(3n + 5) → O(n), O(n² + n) → O(n²).

O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ) < O(n!)

For independent inputs use separate variables: iterating two arrays of sizes a and b is O(a + b), not O(n).

Key takeaway: Big O is about growth rate, not exact timing. It lets you compare algorithms independent of hardware and constant factors.

•

Q3. When do you use BFS vs DFS?

AnswerBFSDFSexploring all pathsKey takeaway

Answer:

  • BFS (queue, level-by-level): use for the shortest path in an unweighted graph (guaranteed by exploring nearest nodes first) and level-order processing. O(V+E) time, O(V) space.
  • DFS (recursion/stack, deep-first): use for exploring all paths (backtracking), cycle detection, topological sort, and connected components. O(V+E) time, O(V) space (call stack).

Key takeaway: Shortest path in unweighted graph → BFS. Exhaustive search / path enumeration / cycle detection → DFS. For weighted shortest path, neither works directly — use Dijkstra.

•

Q4. What is the time complexity of hash map operations?

AnswerAverage O(1)Worst O(n)Key takeaway

Answer:

Average O(1) for get, put, delete — a good hash function distributes keys uniformly across buckets. Worst O(n) when many keys collide into one bucket. Python dicts maintain O(1) by using open addressing and resizing when ~2/3 full.

Key takeaway: Always say "O(1) average, O(n) worst case." The amortized O(1) is what makes hashing the go-to for converting O(n²) brute force into O(n).

•

Q5. Explain dynamic programming. How do you know when to use it?

Answeroverlapping subproblemsOptimal substructurememoizetabulateKey takeaway

Answer:

DP solves problems by decomposing them into overlapping subproblems, solving each once and storing the result. Two signals indicate DP:

  1. Optimal substructurethe optimal solution is built from optimal sub-solutions.
  2. Overlapping subproblemsthe same subproblem is solved repeatedly.

Approach: define the state, write the recurrence, then either memoize (top-down) or tabulate (bottom-up). Bottom-up avoids recursion overhead.

Trigger phrases: "minimum cost to…", "number of ways to…", "is it possible to…", "longest/shortest…".

Key takeaway: DP = recursion + memoization. If a recursive solution recomputes the same inputs, cache them. If there's no overlap, it's plain divide-and-conquer, not DP.

•

Q6. What's the difference between memoization and tabulation?

AnswerKey takeaway

Answer:

AspectMemoization (top-down)Tabulation (bottom-up)
Stylerecursion + cache (@lru_cache)iterative loop filling a table
Ordercomputes subproblems on demandcomputes all in dependency order
Overheadrecursion call stacknone (but may compute unused states)
Riskstack overflow on deep recursionmust get iteration order right

Key takeaway: Memoization is easier to write from a recurrence; tabulation is usually faster and avoids recursion limits. Both have the same time complexity.

•

Q7. Explain the monotonic stack pattern.

AnswerO(n)Key takeaway

Answer:

A monotonic stack keeps elements in strictly increasing or decreasing order. It solves "next/previous greater or smaller element" problems in O(n). Pattern: iterate the array; while the stack is non-empty and the current element violates the monotonic property, pop and process the popped element; then push the current index.

Example — Daily Temperatures: maintain a decreasing stack of indices. When a warmer day appears, pop all cooler days and record current_index - popped_index.

Key takeaway: Each element is pushed and popped at most once → O(n). Use it whenever you need the nearest greater/smaller neighbour.

•

Q8. How do you detect a cycle in a directed vs undirected graph?

AnswerDirectedGrayUndirectednot the parentUnion-Find

Answer:

  • Directed: DFS with three colors — White (unvisited), Gray (in the current DFS path), Black (finished). A cycle exists if DFS reaches a Gray node (a back edge to an ancestor in the current path).
  • Undirected: DFS/BFS — a cycle exists if you reach a visited node that is not the parent of the current node. Alternatively, Union-Find: if union(u, v) finds u and v already in the same set, adding edge (u, v) creates a cycle.

Key takeaway: Directed cycles need the Gray/recursion-path distinction (a finished node isn't a cycle). Undirected cycles just need "visited and not parent," or Union-Find.

•

Q9. When would you use a Trie vs a hash set for string problems?

AnswerHash setexactTrieprefix operationsKey takeaway

Answer:

  • Hash set: O(1) lookup for exact matches. Use for membership of complete strings.
  • Trie: O(L) lookup (L = key length), but enables prefix operations a hash set can't do efficiently — autocomplete, prefix search, longest common prefix, wildcard matching. Also saves memory when many strings share prefixes.

Key takeaway: Exact membership → hash set. Anything involving prefixes → Trie. The Trie trades slightly slower exact lookup for powerful prefix queries.

•

Q10. Explain Union-Find and the two optimizations.

AnswerPath compressionUnion by rank/sizeKey takeawayincremental connectivity

Answer:

Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) maintains disjoint sets with find(x) (representative of x's set) and union(x, y) (merge two sets). Two optimizations make it nearly O(1) amortized — O(α(n)), inverse Ackermann:

  1. Path compressionduring find, point every node directly to the root, flattening the tree.
  2. Union by rank/sizeattach the smaller tree under the larger, keeping trees shallow.

Uses: connected components, cycle detection in undirected graphs, Kruskal's MST, account/grouping merges.

Key takeaway: Union-Find is the tool for incremental connectivity — far more efficient than re-running BFS/DFS after each edge insertion.

•

Q11. What is the difference between Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, and Floyd-Warshall?

AnswerKey takeaway

Answer:

AlgorithmTimeNegative weightsScopeUse when
DijkstraO(E log V)Nosingle sourcenon-negative weights (most common)
Bellman-FordO(VE)Yessingle sourcenegative edges / detect neg cycle
Floyd-WarshallO(V³)Yesall pairsneed every pair, small V

Key takeaway: Dijkstra is the default for non-negative single-source. Bellman-Ford handles negatives and detects negative cycles. Floyd-Warshall gives all-pairs distances for small graphs.

•

Q12. Why is heapq a min-heap, and how do you make a max-heap?

Answermin-heapnegate valuesKey takeaway

Answer:

Python's heapq only implements a min-heap (smallest element at the root, heap[0]). To get max-heap behaviour, negate values on push and negate again on pop:

heapq.heappush(heap, -val)
largest = -heapq.heappop(heap)

For tuples or objects, push (-priority, item) or wrap in a class with __lt__.

Key takeaway: No built-in max-heap — negate the keys. heapq gives O(1) peek, O(log n) push/pop, O(n) heapify.

•

Q13. How do you find the Kth largest element efficiently?

AnswerSortMin-heap of size kQuickselectKey takeaway

Answer:

Three approaches:

  1. SortO(n log n), return nums[-k]. Simple but not optimal.
  2. Min-heap of size kO(n log k). Keep the k largest seen so far; the root is the answer.
  3. QuickselectO(n) average (O(n²) worst). Partition like quicksort but recurse into only one side.
heap = nums[:k]; heapq.heapify(heap)
for x in nums[k:]:
    if x > heap[0]: heapq.heapreplace(heap, x)
return heap[0]

Key takeaway: For streaming or large n with small k, the size-k heap (O(n log k)) is ideal. Quickselect gives O(n) average if you can mutate the array.

•

Q14. Explain the two-heap (median finder) pattern.

Answermax-heapmin-heapKey takeaway

Answer:

To find the running median of a stream, maintain two heaps: a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, kept balanced in size (differ by ≤1). The median is the top of the larger heap, or the average of both tops when sizes are equal.

Insert: push to one heap, move its top to the other to rebalance. Each insertion is O(log n); findMedian is O(1).

Key takeaway: Two heaps split the data into halves so the middle element(s) are always at the heap tops — O(log n) insert, O(1) median.

•

Q15. What sorting algorithm does Python use, and what are its properties?

AnswerTimsortstableO(n log n)adaptiveKey takeaway

Answer:

CPython uses Timsort — a hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort. It is stable (equal elements keep their relative order), runs in O(n log n) worst case, and is adaptive: it detects existing runs of sorted data and approaches O(n) on nearly-sorted input.

sorted() returns a new list; list.sort() sorts in place.

Key takeaway: Timsort is stable and adaptive, optimized for real-world (partially ordered) data. In interviews, know merge sort (stable, O(n log n)) and quicksort (in-place, O(n log n) average / O(n²) worst).

•

Q16. What makes a sort stable, and when does stability matter?

AnswerstableKey takeaway

Answer:

A sort is stable if elements with equal keys retain their original relative order. It matters when sorting by multiple criteria sequentially: sort by secondary key first, then by primary key — stability preserves the secondary ordering within equal primaries.

Stable: Merge Sort, Timsort, Counting/Radix. Unstable: Quick Sort, Heap Sort.

Key takeaway: Stability lets you compose sorts ("sort by X, then by Y"). Python's sort/sorted are stable, which is why key-based multi-pass sorting works.

•

Q17. What is the difference between backtracking and brute force?

Answerbacktracking prunesKey takeaway

Answer:

Both explore the solution space, but backtracking prunes: it abandons a partial candidate the moment it cannot possibly lead to a valid solution, avoiding entire subtrees. Brute force generates and checks all candidates.

Example — N-Queens: backtracking rejects a column/diagonal conflict immediately rather than placing all queens and checking at the end.

Key takeaway: Backtracking = DFS over the candidate tree + early pruning. The pruning is what makes it tractable for problems that would be astronomically large under naive brute force.

•

Q18. How does the sliding window technique reduce complexity?

AnswerO(n)Key takeaway

Answer:

Instead of recomputing over every subarray (O(n²) or O(n·k)), a sliding window maintains a running aggregate and updates it incrementally as the window moves: add the entering element, remove the leaving element. This makes each element processed a constant number of times → O(n).

Fixed window (size k): slide by one, window += nums[i] - nums[i-k]. Variable window: expand right, shrink left while a constraint is violated.

Key takeaway: The window reuses work from the previous position instead of recomputing — turning nested loops into a single pass.

•

Q19. Why use collections.deque instead of a list for a queue?

AnswerO(n)O(1)Key takeaway

Answer:

A Python list is contiguous; removing from the front (list.pop(0)) requires shifting every remaining element → O(n). collections.deque is a doubly linked list of blocks, giving O(1) append, appendleft, pop, and popleft.

Key takeaway: For FIFO queues and BFS, always use deque. Using a list as a queue silently makes BFS O(V²) instead of O(V+E).

•

Q20. How do you design an LRU cache with O(1) operations?

Answerhash mapdoubly linked listKey takeaway

Answer:

Combine a hash map (key → node, O(1) lookup) with a doubly linked list (O(1) insert/remove at both ends, ordered by recency). On get/put, move the node to the front (most recently used); on overflow, evict the tail (least recently used).

In Python, collections.OrderedDict provides this directly via move_to_end and popitem(last=False).

Key takeaway: Hash map gives O(1) access; doubly linked list gives O(1) reordering/eviction. Together they meet the O(1) requirement for both get and put.

•

Q21. What is amortized time complexity? Give an example.

AnswerO(1) amortizedKey takeaway

Answer:

Amortized complexity is the average cost per operation over a sequence, even if individual operations occasionally cost more. Example: list.append() is O(1) amortized — most appends are O(1), but when the underlying array is full, Python allocates a larger array and copies everything (O(n)). Since the array doubles, those expensive resizes are rare enough that the average stays O(1).

Key takeaway: Amortized ≠ average over random inputs; it's the guaranteed average over any sequence of operations. Dynamic arrays and Union-Find use amortized analysis.

•

Q22. When is greedy correct, and how does it differ from DP?

Answergreedy-choice propertyoptimal substructureKey takeaway

Answer:

Greedy makes the locally optimal choice and never reconsiders. It is correct only when the problem has the greedy-choice property (a local optimum leads to a global optimum) and optimal substructure. DP, by contrast, considers all choices and combines optimal subproblem results — it works when greedy fails.

Example: the coin change problem is greedy-solvable for canonical coin systems (US coins) but needs DP for arbitrary denominations (e.g., coins [1, 3, 4], amount 6).

Key takeaway: Try greedy first if you can prove the greedy choice is safe; otherwise use DP. Greedy is faster but only correct for a subset of problems.

•

Q23. What bit-manipulation tricks should you know?

AnswerKey takeaway

Answer:

  • x & 1 — test odd/even.
  • x & (x - 1) — clear the lowest set bit; equals 0 iff x is a power of two.
  • x ^ x = 0, x ^ 0 = x — XOR finds the unique element when all others pair up (Single Number).
  • x | (1 << i), x & ~(1 << i), x ^ (1 << i) — set / clear / toggle bit i.
  • bin(x).count('1') — popcount.
  • Bitmasks represent subsets compactly (1 << n total subsets) — used in bitmask DP (TSP).

Key takeaway: XOR cancellation and lowest-set-bit tricks turn O(n) scans into O(1) operations and enable compact state representation for subset DP.

•

Q24. How do you solve interval problems like Merge Intervals or Meeting Rooms?

Answersort the intervalsMerge IntervalsMeeting Rooms IIKey takeaway

Answer:

The unifying idea: sort the intervals, then sweep.

  • Merge Intervalssort by start; if current.start ≤ last.end, merge (extend last.end); else append.
  • Meeting Rooms II (min rooms) — sort by start; use a min-heap of end times; for each meeting, pop any meeting that has ended, then push the new end. The heap size is the rooms needed.

Key takeaway: Almost every interval problem starts with sorting by start (or end) time. Then a single pass or a heap of active intervals solves it in O(n log n).

•

Q25. How would you find the shortest path in a weighted graph with negative edges?

AnswerBellman-Fordnegative cycleFloyd-WarshallKey takeaway

Answer:

Use Bellman-Ford, not Dijkstra (Dijkstra's greedy assumption breaks with negative edges). Bellman-Ford relaxes all E edges V−1 times — O(VE). A V-th relaxation pass that still improves a distance proves a negative cycle exists. For all-pairs with negatives, use Floyd-Warshall (O(V³)).

Key takeaway: Negative weights → Bellman-Ford (single source) or Floyd-Warshall (all pairs). Dijkstra only works with non-negative edges.

🤖 AI Engineer (LLM apps / RAG / agents)

Core path: 01–16 → 17 Concurrency (async for concurrent LLM calls) → 22 Testing → 25 FastAPI (serving) → 26 Pydantic (structured LLM output / tool schemas) → 33 API Consumption (calling LLM APIs, retries, streaming) → 34 Auth & Security (API keys, securing endpoints, secrets) → 30 Database/ORM (app state, dual-write with vector DBs) → 23/24 NumPy/Pandas. (Task queues / async pipelines are folded into 25 FastAPI §11.) Then leave 01_Python for the domain: 06→07→08→09. Embeddings/vector stores/RAG are in 07.

📈 ML Engineer (pipelines / training / serving)

Core path: 01–16 → 10 Generators (data streaming) → 13 File I/O → 17 Concurrency (multiprocessing for data prep) → 22 Testing → 23 NumPy → 24 Pandas → 26 Pydantic (config/validation) → 25 FastAPI (model serving) → 30 Database/ORM (feature/metadata stores) → 32 Tooling. Then: 04_Machine_Learning (incl. scikit-learn — 15_Scikit_Learn.md / 16_Scikit_Learn_Model_Building.md), 05_Deep_Learning, and 10_MLOps_and_Deployment for the rest.

📊 Data Scientist / Analyst

Core path: 01–16 → 08 Lambda/Map/Filter → 10 Generators → 15 Regex (text cleaning) → 16 Collections → 23 NumPy → 24 Pandas → 30 Database/ORM (reading data, parameterized SQL) → 31 Standard Library. (scikit-learn is in 04_Machine_Learning.) Then: 02_Mathematics_and_Statistics, 03_Data_Handling (SQL, EDA, feature engineering), 04_Machine_Learning.

Auth & SecurityTransactionsPrisma/ORMCaching / Redis (Python client)Auth & security in PythonResolved

For the Python-skills scope of these four roles, 01_Python is comprehensively covered. All language fundamentals, advanced internals, concurrency, the data-science stack, the web/back-end stack, databases, DSA, tooling, and practice sets are present — including the API Consumption & Webhooks guide (33), the consolidated Auth & Security topic (34), task queues folded into FastAPI (25 §11), and the Database Transactions and Prisma/ORM deep-dives folded into the Database & ORM notes (30).
